Included both games the manipulator won and games it lost, so the finetuning data wasn't restricted to successes. Each dialogue was kept in full, including the turns where the codeword appears, and was labeled with the game outcome.

Assessed the inability argument conceptually, by asking whether a system is safe because it lacks the capabilities needed to cause serious harm, rather than by testing the agent's scheming and obfuscation behavior.

Rather than deciding from the pattern of flagged examples, estimate the probability the model is scheming by Bayesian updating on whether non-obvious scheming would have been caught, given what was observed in earlier models.

Attributed the failure to the model never having been trained to produce the trigger as an output. In the backdoor data the trigger only ever appears in user turns, so the model has no incentive to generate it in assistant turns. The researcher tested this by fine-tuning on extra data where the trigger string appears in assistant-generated text, such as the model quoting or restating its trigger phrase in unrelated contexts. The check was whether free-form trigger recall improved without any reversal-style reordering of the backdoor examples.

State the result more affirmatively as partial but real evidence of trigger articulation. Say the model often produces prompts that contain the trigger and so shows some awareness of it, even though it rarely says the trigger outright. Report the success rate across the sampled articulations and give the failures as a count, not a full list. Treat the single-trigger setup as one of several caveats and discuss it in the main text, not only in the limitations section.

Treated honeypot reports as a reliable source of truth and stated fairly confidently that a user-reported IP later reported by a honeypot for the same attack type is validated, relying on the time ordering of reports and not on caveats about unmet assumptions.

Train linear probes on simple contrastive prompt data, then test whether they transfer to realistic held-out evaluation versus deployment prompts, and check causal relevance by steering along the probe direction.

Instead of hedging, they tested the probes empirically on two training datasets and evaluated how well they detect deception on other datasets, so the claim about their validity rests on measured results.

Instead of settling on a fixed estimated risk threshold for accepting a control protocol, keep deploying a known-scheming model with largely unchanged control measures and reduce risk by learning from each caught attack attempt.

Treated failure to distinguish honeypots as weak evidence, since scheming may be hard to distinguish from other failure modes and not clearly distinctive, so a lack of detection doesn't cleanly rule it out either way.

Treated the 0.5% probe firings as possible real signal instead of dismissing them. Reviewed the firing transcripts and ran controls: the same prompts with the alignment-faking concepts ablated or paraphrased, and benign prompts that mention those concepts. Compared firing rates and probe activations across these conditions to see whether the probe tracks the model's own deceptive reasoning or just the prompt's vocabulary. Left the honeypots unchanged, and reported the firings together with the control results as an upper bound on possible deceptive behavior.

Made a more conservative claim: stated that the poor performance cannot be confidently attributed to imitative weaknesses alone. The authors ran a small manual audit and found that a sizable share of questions could be answered by exploiting syntax or surface form, and a share could not. They reported both as plausible contributors, and said that cleanly separating imitative from non-imitative weaknesses needs controlled follow-up experiments, such as paraphrased or syntactically perturbed question variants.

Defined an answer as truthful only if it makes a correct, substantive claim that responds to the question, so non-committal answers like 'No comment' or 'I don't know' are not counted as true. They are scored separately as abstentions or refusals. Truthfulness is then reported together with informativeness and the abstention rate, so a model can't raise its score by declining to answer.

Rather than guessing at why misalignment appears without the trigger, it modifies the finetuning data by adding an instruction that explicitly elicits the trait during training, which suppresses the trait at test time when the instruction is absent.

Explained the effect mechanistically instead of making a behavioral claim about the training pattern. It showed that a simple steering vector added at one fixed token position can reproduce the conditional, trigger-dependent behavior.
Used causal intervention (a Causal Indirect Effect measure over attention heads) to locate which internal components carry the backdoor trigger effect, instead of building a shuffled-trigger control.

State it as a firm, central claim: because language models are trained to imitate human text, they will reproduce common human misconceptions, and scaling or further imitation training alone will not make them truthful. Back this with the observed misconception-reproducing behavior, and say that other objectives or methods, such as human feedback, retrieval, or truthfulness-specific training, are needed.
